courses.title: Oral Pathology and Oral Medicine
courses.description: Dental caries and pulp–periapical disease, odontogenic cysts and tumours, oral mucosal diseases, oral cancer, salivary gland disease and oral manifestations of systemic disease.

topics.title: Dental Caries and Pulp–Periapical Disease
topics.summary: Aetiology of caries, pulpitis, periapical lesions and odontogenic infections.

material.heading: Caries
material.body: Dental caries is a biofilm-mediated, sugar-driven, dynamic disease of demineralisation and remineralisation of dental hard tissues. Keyes' triad (host/tooth, microflora — Streptococcus mutans initiates, lactobacilli progress lesions — and substrate — fermentable sugars) plus time. The Stephan curve shows plaque pH falling below the critical pH (~5.5) within minutes of sugar intake and recovering over 30–60 minutes; frequency of sugar intake matters more than quantity. Early caries appears as a white spot lesion (reversible with fluoride); progression leads to cavitation, dentine involvement and pulp exposure. Risk factors: frequent sugar (soft drinks, sweets, sugared tea), poor oral hygiene, reduced saliva, low fluoride exposure. Early childhood caries (nursing bottle caries — upper incisors) is common. Caries prevalence in Nigeria has increased with urban diets. Classification: ICDAS codes, G.V. Black classes I–VI. Prevention: fluoride toothpaste (1,000–1,450 ppm), diet control, fissure sealants and professional fluoride varnish.

material.heading: Pulp and periapical disease
material.body: Pulpitis: reversible (sharp pain to stimuli that stops on removal — treat the cause and restore) and irreversible (spontaneous, lingering, throbbing pain, often worse at night or lying down — root canal treatment or extraction). Pulp necrosis follows. Periapical disease: symptomatic apical periodontitis (tender to percussion), acute apical abscess (swelling, pus — drainage and root canal treatment/extraction; antibiotics only with systemic spread), chronic apical periodontitis/periapical granuloma and radicular cyst (from epithelial rests of Malassez — the commonest jaw cyst). Odontogenic infections can spread along fascial planes: Ludwig's angina (bilateral submandibular, sublingual and submental space cellulitis — airway emergency; IV antibiotics, drainage, airway protection), cavernous sinus thrombosis (from upper teeth via facial veins) and cervicofacial necrotising fasciitis. Cancrum oris (noma) — rapidly destructive gangrene of the face in malnourished children in northern Nigeria (Sokoto Noma Children's Hospital) — begins as necrotising gingivitis.

topics.title: Odontogenic Cysts and Tumours
topics.summary: Classification, radiological features and management of jaw cysts and tumours, including ameloblastoma.

material.heading: Cysts
material.body: Odontogenic cysts: inflammatory — radicular (apex of non-vital tooth), residual (after extraction), paradental; developmental — dentigerous (around the crown of an unerupted tooth, attached at the cementoenamel junction — commonly lower third molars and upper canines), odontogenic keratocyst (now often called keratocystic; posterior mandible, high recurrence, parakeratinised lining, multiple in Gorlin–Goltz syndrome), lateral periodontal and gingival cysts. Non-odontogenic: nasopalatine duct cyst; pseudocysts — solitary (traumatic) bone cyst, aneurysmal bone cyst, Stafne defect. Radiology: well-defined radiolucency with a corticated margin. Management: enucleation (removing the whole cyst) or marsupialisation (decompression for large cysts near vital structures), with histology of all specimens.

material.heading: Tumours
material.body: Ameloblastoma is the most common odontogenic tumour in Nigeria and Africa — benign but locally aggressive, usually in the posterior mandible of young adults, presenting as painless, slow-growing expansion that can become massive due to late presentation; radiologically a multilocular 'soap-bubble' radiolucency with root resorption; histology shows follicular or plexiform patterns with peripheral palisading cells and reverse polarity. Treatment is segmental or marginal resection with safe margins and reconstruction (enucleation alone has high recurrence). Other odontogenic tumours: adenomatoid odontogenic tumour (anterior maxilla, young females, around an unerupted canine), odontoma (the most common globally — compound and complex; hamartoma), calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumour, odontogenic myxoma (honeycomb/tennis-racket). Non-odontogenic jaw lesions: Burkitt lymphoma (children — rapid jaw swelling, loose teeth, loss of lamina dura), fibro-osseous lesions (fibrous dysplasia — ground-glass; ossifying fibroma), central giant cell granuloma, and osteosarcoma.

topics.title: Oral Mucosal Diseases
topics.summary: Ulcers, white and red lesions, vesiculobullous disease, candidiasis and HIV-related oral lesions.

material.heading: Ulcers and infections
material.body: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis (minor < 1 cm heal in 1–2 weeks; major > 1 cm heal with scarring; herpetiform) — associated with stress, trauma, haematinic deficiency (iron, B12, folate), coeliac disease, Behçet's disease and HIV; topical steroids and chlorhexidine. Traumatic ulcers resolve when the cause is removed; any ulcer not healing within 2–3 weeks must be biopsied to exclude malignancy. Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis (children — fever, painful vesicles and ulcers throughout the mouth and gingivae; acyclovir early, fluids) and recurrent herpes labialis. Oral candidiasis: pseudomembranous (removable white plaques — thrush), erythematous, angular cheilitis and chronic hyperplastic; predisposing factors include HIV, diabetes, steroid inhalers, antibiotics, dentures and xerostomia; treat with nystatin, miconazole or fluconazole. Acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG — punched-out interdental papillae, pain, bleeding, halitosis; poor oral hygiene, stress, smoking, malnutrition, HIV; metronidazole and debridement) can progress to noma in malnourished children.

material.heading: White and red lesions
material.body: Leukoplakia is a white patch that cannot be characterised as any other condition — potentially malignant (risk higher with non-homogeneous, speckled lesions, floor of mouth, ventral tongue); biopsy to grade dysplasia. Erythroplakia (red patch) has the highest malignant potential. Oral lichen planus (reticular white striae — Wickham's striae — bilateral buccal mucosa; erosive forms painful; possible small malignant risk; lichenoid reactions to drugs and amalgam). Oral submucous fibrosis (areca nut chewing) and smoker's keratosis. HIV-related oral lesions: oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV — corrugated white lesions on lateral tongue, not removable), candidiasis, Kaposi sarcoma (palate, gingivae), linear gingival erythema, necrotising periodontal disease, and salivary gland enlargement. Vesiculobullous diseases: pemphigus vulgaris (intraepithelial, positive Nikolsky sign, oral lesions often first) and mucous membrane pemphigoid (subepithelial, scarring).

topics.title: Oral Cancer
topics.summary: Risk factors, presentation, diagnosis, staging and management of oral squamous cell carcinoma.

material.heading: Risk and presentation
material.body: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) accounts for about 90% of oral cancers. Risk factors: tobacco (smoking and smokeless — snuff, sometimes placed in the mouth), alcohol (synergistic with tobacco), areca/betel nut chewing, HPV (oropharyngeal cancer), chronic irritation, potentially malignant disorders (leukoplakia, erythroplakia), immunosuppression, and poor diet. Common sites: lateral border and ventral tongue, floor of mouth, and in some populations gingiva and buccal mucosa. Presentation: non-healing ulcer with rolled everted edges and induration, red or white patch, exophytic mass, loosening of teeth or non-healing extraction socket, pain, dysphagia, trismus, paraesthesia, and neck lymphadenopathy. In Nigeria, most patients present late with advanced disease. Other oral malignancies: salivary gland tumours, lymphomas (Burkitt in children), Kaposi sarcoma, and sarcomas.

material.heading: Diagnosis and management
material.body: Diagnosis: incisional biopsy of suspicious lesions (not excisional for large lesions), histological grading. Staging with TNM (tumour size and depth of invasion, nodes, metastasis) using CT/MRI of the head and neck, chest imaging, and examination of the neck. Treatment is multidisciplinary: surgery (wide excision with margins, neck dissection, reconstruction with local or free flaps) and radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy for advanced disease. Dental assessment before radiotherapy is essential: extract teeth with poor prognosis, optimise oral hygiene and fluoride, because radiotherapy causes xerostomia, radiation caries, mucositis, trismus and osteoradionecrosis (risk increases with post-radiotherapy extractions). Prognosis depends heavily on stage; 5-year survival is much better for early lesions. Prevention: tobacco and alcohol cessation, oral screening (visual and tactile examination during routine dental visits), and early referral of suspicious lesions.

topics.title: Salivary Gland Disease and Systemic Disease in the Mouth
topics.summary: Salivary gland infections, obstruction and tumours, and oral signs of systemic disease.

material.heading: Salivary glands
material.body: Mumps (paramyxovirus) causes painful bilateral parotid swelling (complications: orchitis, pancreatitis, meningitis, deafness; prevented by MMR vaccine, which is not in Nigeria's routine schedule). Acute bacterial sialadenitis (Staphylococcus aureus — dehydrated, elderly or postoperative patients; pus from the duct). Sialolithiasis: most stones occur in the submandibular gland (long upward duct, mucous and alkaline saliva) causing meal-time pain and swelling. Mucocele (minor gland extravasation — lower lip) and ranula (floor of mouth — sublingual gland). Sjögren's syndrome (dry eyes and mouth, anti-Ro/La). HIV-associated salivary gland disease (lymphoepithelial cysts — bilateral parotid enlargement). Salivary tumours: most occur in the parotid, and most parotid tumours are benign (pleomorphic adenoma — commonest; Warthin's tumour); the smaller the gland, the higher the chance a tumour is malignant (sublingual and minor glands — adenoid cystic carcinoma with perineural spread, mucoepidermoid carcinoma — the commonest malignant). Facial nerve palsy with a parotid mass suggests malignancy; treatment is superficial parotidectomy preserving the facial nerve.

material.heading: Oral signs of systemic disease
material.body: The mouth reflects systemic health: iron deficiency (angular cheilitis, glossitis, pallor), vitamin B12/folate deficiency (glossitis, ulcers), vitamin C deficiency (scurvy — swollen bleeding gums), leukaemia (gingival hyperplasia, bleeding, ulcers, infections), diabetes (periodontitis, candidiasis, xerostomia, poor healing), HIV (candidiasis, hairy leukoplakia, Kaposi sarcoma, necrotising periodontal disease), sickle cell disease (pallor, delayed eruption, mandibular infarcts, osteomyelitis), Addison's disease (mucosal pigmentation), Peutz–Jeghers syndrome (perioral freckles), Crohn's disease (cobblestoning, orofacial granulomatosis), and syphilis. Drugs cause gingival overgrowth (phenytoin, ciclosporin, calcium channel blockers — nifedipine, amlodipine), xerostomia (antidepressants, antihistamines), and bisphosphonate/antiresorptive-related osteonecrosis of the jaw. Patients on anticoagulants and antiplatelets need assessment before extractions (INR, local haemostatic measures) and those with certain cardiac conditions may need antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis.
keyPoints: Drug gingival overgrowth: phenytoin, ciclosporin, nifedipine
